prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its biologically active form, which made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration: I now propose Drucker, Holst and Mojsov for B049 as a single-part prize, replacing Knudsen with Mojsov. The scientific case is unchanged and rests on the arc from the incretin effect in humans, through the biologically active truncated GLP-1 and the proglucagon-derived peptide and receptor biology, to drugs with large benefit in type 2 diabetes, obesity and, in randomized outcome trials, cardiovascular and renal disease. The mechanism has been confirmed independently for decades, so there is no maturity concern. What moved me is the question of what the Prize is for. Five colleagues independently reached the same trio on the principle that a physiological discovery, not the engineering of a drug, decides the seats. My round-1 case for Knudsen depended on treating acylation-based half-life extension as a conceptually new step. I still think it was a real scientific advance, but I accept that it is a step in realizing a mechanism that others had already defined, and that it was achieved inside an industrial team, which makes individual credit harder to state in a citation. I said in round 1 that Knudsen's seat is the weakest if discovery decides, and the room has now made that argument. Development is not ignored: the citation says explicitly that the discoveries made incretin-based therapies possible, which answers the concern of Perlmann and Wahren-Herlenius that a physiology-only citation would look indifferent to the medicine.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakness, and my change does not remove it. The Mojsov seat carries the priority question for the active peptide, which overlaps with Habener's group. Habener is outside the credited names and would be omitted from a three-seat prize that can fairly be called incomplete. No one in this exchange, including me, has produced primary documents that settle it: we are all working from recollection of the history. I move to Mojsov because I judge the purpose of the Prize to favour her over Knudsen, not because I think her priority is settled. The trio also leaves out Knudsen, whose work made the medicine practical for millions, so the citation will be criticized as favouring the hormone over the drug. Finally, the standard is only defensible if we apply it consistently: if discovery decides here, it should also decide for imatinib and CAR-T, and I accept that consequence.

responses.point: Linnarsson keeps Mojsov over Knudsen, arguing that the prize honours the discovery that opened a field and that the active peptide is the entity every later drug is built on, while conceding that this is a judgment about the purpose of the Prize and not about who did more work.
responses.response: I now agree with you, and for your reason. Your framing of it as a judgment about purpose is the honest one. My objection in round 1 was that Mojsov's priority is entangled with Habener's group. I still hold that, but it is a risk to manage and not a reason to put a development contribution into a discovery seat. Your point that development credit rests on a large industrial team also matters: a laureate seat has to be defensible in one sentence of a citation. I withdraw my statement that Knudsen's contribution is the least disputed, since being undisputed is not the same as being the discovery.

responses.point: Perlmann would credit Mojsov, wants the citation to name incretin-based therapy explicitly, and would want the priority question resolved before accepting Knudsen if the committee chose to recognise development.
responses.response: Your suggestion on the citation settles most of what separates us. Naming incretin-based therapy while crediting the physiological discoveries answers my concern about ignoring the medicine without putting a drug developer in a discovery seat, so I have adopted that wording. On your demand that the priority question be settled, I cannot do that from documents. I can say that the dispute with Habener's group concerns who established the activity of the truncated peptide first, not whether the discovery occurred, and that is a dispute of degree. If the committee finds it cannot be defended against the primary literature, the weakness lies with the whole trio, and I would want that tested before the vote.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius asks for a consistent discovery-versus-development standard across GLP-1, imatinib and CAR-T, and notes that a prize this obvious should be tested against the line we apply to others.
responses.response: I accept that test and apply it to my own change. Under a discovery standard B049 passes through the incretin physiology and the active peptide. B011 is weaker, because its central step is a drug against a target already known, and B014 rests on an engineering achievement, the costimulated receptor, with a clinical proof. Applying the standard strictly would put B049 ahead of both, and that is where my ranking stays. I also accept the consequence that Knudsen's exclusion is a standard I would have to defend elsewhere.

responses.point: Svenningsson would keep Mojsov over Knudsen because the category concerns discovery of physiological principles and Holst and Drucker already carry the chain to the therapeutic rationale, but could accept Knudsen if the committee wished to recognise development and said so openly in the citation.
responses.response: I agree with the first half and have moved to it. Your point that the identification of the active form is what made any analogue design meaningful is the strongest argument for the seat. I do not need your fallback, because I now think the citation can acknowledge the therapies without crediting their developer. Your statement that the choice is contestable and that the citation should not pretend otherwise is one I share. I would keep the citation modest on priority and say 'discoveries of' the physiology and the active form, not 'the discovery of', so that it does not assert a sole first claim.

responses.point: El-Manira holds Mojsov over Knudsen because the Prize is for the discovery and Knudsen's work is pharmaceutical optimization of an existing mechanism, and asks whether anyone considers the Mojsov priority question settled.
responses.response: I cannot say it is settled and I will not pretend to. I also need to correct my round-1 response to you: I wrote that you and Linnarsson shared unease about conduct questions concerning a credited individual in the TOR ballot, but your round-1 statement does not say that, and I should not have attributed it to you. I cannot support it from anything I have read, so I withdraw it as a factor and set it aside. B001 stays a second alternative on the science only, around Hall, with attribution still an open matter. On Mojsov, we agree on the purpose of the Prize and on the unresolved priority question, and my disagreement with you has narrowed to calling acylation conceptually new, which I regard as a smaller dispute.

uncertainties: Whether the priority of the active truncated GLP-1 can be defended against the primary literature, including the role of Habener's group, which I still know only from memory and not from verified documents.
Whether the citation wording on the active form and on incretin-based therapy credits the physiologists without overstating priority, and without appearing to dismiss Knudsen's contribution.
Whether a two-part prize pairing B049 with B014 could work within three names; I see no way to do it without weakening the GLP-1 attribution, so I propose a single part.
Whether, if CAR-T is pursued in the final ballot, the June and Sadelain pair and a citation worded around engineered costimulated receptors can fairly handle Eshhar's absence.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited candidate on the shortlist. My profile documents co-authorship with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisén and a shared Karolinska Institutet setting, and a long-standing member of my lab, none of which bears on any shortlisted topic. I am correcting the attribution made in my round-1 response about conduct concerns in B001: it is not supported by anything I have read.
